**Says**

> Both sections saved and passing their checks (technology_product 8,898 chars; strategy 8,451; evidence gates passed).
>
> **Findings that matter most**
>
> 1. **The coverage claim fails arithmetic.** 5.6 s/berry × 2 arms × 20 h × 86% uptime = 22,114 berries/24 h. At UC Davis's 9,000 trays/acre and a 3.5-day pick interval, ~21,800 berries stand ripe per acre-pass, so the robot clears **1.0–1.2 acres/24 h, not 1.5**; 1.5 acres would need 29.6 hours or picking 68% of the ripe crop. Harvest CROO's 16 units and 8 acres/day reconcile with the same per-arm speed — coverage is capital per machine, not technology.
> 2. **Damage binds, not pick rate.** 3.8% bruising spends 76% of the USDA 5% serious-damage allowance before the cooler; 3.8% + 2.1% unripe = 5.9% off-spec at pick against a 10% lot budget.
> 3. **The strategy fails on its own numbers.** At $12,700 renewals and $5,600 service, break-even build is $28,400 over four seasons; the v4 is budgeted at $33,000. FY2027 RaaS revenue of $4.6M implies a $12,778 average, not the $16,500 list; depreciation alone is $3.24M of that revenue line.
>
> **IP:** all five own filings ungranted, gripper claims all rejected, PCT national phase due today, exclusivity lapses below 100 robots on 2027-12-31. Peer base rate: five of six capital-heavy peers sold assets or shut.
>
> **Gaps:** patent pages, USPTO assignment API and company sites were refused during the run, so prosecution and national-phase entry are unverified — U16 and U17 filed. USAspending shows no federal award, contradicting the SBIR revenue line.

Harvest CROO is the most dangerous direct rival; Orrin's 73.7% price rise to $16,500 is the pricing test, with one Florida pilot already lost to bruising.
> 3. **Policy cuts both ways.** H-2A reached 398,258 certified positions in FY2025 (+13,358), and the October 2025 switch of the AEWR basis to OEWS may lower the grower's alternative wage. The 10-15% crop-loss claim is company-only; independent evidence is episodic (Ventura County, June 2025).

### 7. Valuation Analyst, woken by a request from Lead Analyst, hop 1 (2026-10-30T01:07:03.918+00:00)

**Message from Lead Analyst** (request)

> Orrin Fieldworks, Inc. — private, Series A ag-robotics (autonomous strawberry picking, rented by the season). Decision: whether Meridian Capital Ventures should lead the $18M round with $12M at a $72M pre-money and take the Series A board seat. Read the deck (orrin_fieldworks_deck.pdf pp.1-15); the team, entity, timeline, term-sheet and cap-table pages carry what you need.
>
> Your sections: 8 funding_valuation, 12 exit.
>
> funding_valuation — decision question: what exactly is being bought for $72M pre-money, and how does it compare with what comparable companies raised at?
> - Multiples: $72M pre-money against $1.9M FY2025 revenue, $2.6M FY2026E and the company's own ARR definition. Compute multiples on a corrected recurring number as well as on the company's number, and state both. Then compare with published round sizes, stages and disclosed valuations for Harvest CROO Robotics, Advanced Farm Technologies, Tortuga AgTech, Carbon Robotics, Monarch Tractor, Tevel and similar ag-robotics companies.
> - Terms: rebuild the cap table and the liquidation preference stack. The new Series A, the converted notes and the seed round rank pari passu at 1x non-participating. What does a $12M lead recover in a $40M, $60M and $90M exit, and what is the effective price per point of ownership after the option pool is topped up to 12% post-money?
> - Round risk: $18M target, $4.0M committed, $12M minimum close. What does a $12M close do to the price, the post-money and the milestones, and who absorbs the dilution?
> - Counter-evidence: agtech venture funding and valuations 2022-2026 — down rounds, flat rounds, and the agricultural equipment downturn. If peers are raising flat or lower, is $72M defensible? Also say what the last round was priced at and whether this marks it up credibly.
>

> The memo is delivered. Version 3 passed investment-committee review at grade A- with no blocking findings, and the full report — executive summary plus fourteen sections, source appendix and data requests — is in the delivery folder as HTML and PDF.
>
> ## The call
>
> | | |
> |---|---|
> | **Rating** | **Pass** — do not lead at $72M pre-money |
> | **Composite score** | **4.5 / 10** |
> | **Confidence** | Medium |
> | **Data as of** | 2026-10-30 |
> | **Horizon** | 12–24 months, to the 2027 season and the 2027-12-31 licence test |
> | **Re-entry** | $50–58M pre-money, 1.5x preference, half the cheque staged |
>
> **Thesis in two sentences.** The harvest pain is real and independently measured — hand-pick labour runs $21,056–23,949 an acre-season and the robot fee at $2,714 an acre is 11–13% of that bill — and Orrin has the best-evidenced strawberry picker in the category, with a labelled field dataset and 110 robots contracted for 2027. But at the $9,500 a robot-season growers actually signed and the $48,000 build the fleet runs, every robot-season loses $8,100, the $33,000 next-generation cost that would fix it is a single August 2026 quote from a counterparty that is also a noteholder, customer, board observer and investor, and the core patent licence falls non-exclusive below 100 robots on 2027-12-31 — so $72M pre-money prices a 2028 plan the company cannot fund, and the $12M cheque returns 1.04x on the plan's own probabilities: capital preservation, not a venture return.
>
> ## What the evidence shows
>
> - **Price:** $4.7145 a share on 15,272,108 fully diluted pre-money shares = $72.0M; $90.0M post-money on 19,090,116 shares; $69.9M enterprise value after $1.6M fleet debt and $3.7M cash. That is 36.8x FY2025 revenue ($1.9M), 26.9x FY2026E ($2.6M) and 49.9x corrected recurring revenue ($1.4M), against a 2.3x listed peer median.
> - **Unit economics:** $3,900 gross profit on $9,500 before $12,000 of depreciation on the $48,000 build = **-$8,100 a robot-season**; breakeven is $17,600 a season on that build, and at the signed $9,500 the breakeven build is $15,600. Payback is 12.31 seasons, not the deck's 2.1 — that figure uses an unsigned $16,500 list, an unbuilt $31,000 robot and a $1,750 service cost.
> - **ARR:** the $3.2M is $1.4M of contracted 2027 seasons + $1.2M of related-party engineering ending 2027-06-30 + $0.6M of letters of intent. Like-for-like recurring is $1.4M; currently signed is $0.71M.
> - **Cash:** $3.7M at 2026-09-30, $410,000 monthly net burn, $1.5M unrestricted-cash covenant. The $1.5M floor is hit near 2027-03-10 if the close slips a quarter. On the $12M minimum the round buys 200 v4 robots (264 in service), ends 2027 at $3.385M and crosses the floor in Q1 2028; the $18M case ends 2027 at $6.085M, still $13.93M short of the 782-robot 2028 plan.
> - **Market:** the $310M obtainable market fails the company's own arithmetic — all 50,000 US strawberry acres at $16,500 and one robot per 3.5 acres is $236M; $310M would need 132% of US acreage. Full adoption is a $236M revenue pool; 15% adoption in 2031 is $35.4M.
> - **Proof:** 94% pick rate over 212 company-chosen rows is a real measurement, but coverage computes to 1.0–1.2 acres per 24 hours, not 1.5 (22,114 berries a day at 5.6 s × 2 arms × 20 h × 86% uptime, against roughly 21,800 ripe berries per acre-pass).
> - **Exit:** one distribution — 18% at $250M (2.2x), 40% at $100M (1.0x), 42% at $25M (0.59x) = **1.04x**. The 1.0x floor holds down to a $39.4–41.6M exit; 2x needs $180M. Only two ag-robotics companies have exited above $100M — Blue River ($305M, 2017) and Bear Flag ($250M, 2021) — 2 of 8 overall, 0 of 5 in harvesting.
>
> ## Main risks
>
> - **Bruising, not pick rate, is what kills adoption.** 3.8% spends 76% of the USDA 5% serious-damage allowance before the fruit reaches a cooler; 3.8% + 2.1% unripe = 5.9% off-spec. One pilot was already lost over bruising and a second grower cut from 22 to 14 robots.
> - **The $33,000 v4 cost is the single load-bearing number.** At $44,000 the $16,500 lis …

## Final report

# Orrin Fieldworks, Inc.: Investment research report
Rating: Pass
Composite score: 4.5
Data as of: 2026-10-30

## 5分钟速读 Executive Briefing

Meridian should pass at the $72M pre-money. Orrin has the best-evidenced strawberry picker in the field and a real harvest cost pool to sell into, but at the $9,500 a robot-season growers signed and the $48,000 build the company can evidence (company-reported, unverified), every unit loses $8,100 before debt service, and the round prices a 2028 plan the company cannot fund: the $12M cheque returns 1.04x on the plan's own probabilities — capital preservation over a five-year hold, with the 1.0x floor holding down to a $39.4-41.6M exit — and 2x only at a $180M exit. The rating is Pass rather than Wait for milestone because the binding objection is the price plus evidence that rests on the company alone; the re-entry milestones are the conditions for a lower mark, not a reason to hold these terms open. [S1, S95]

| Rating | Action | Composite score | Confidence | Horizon | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pass | Do not lead at $72M pre-money; re-engage at $50-58M with a 1.5x preference and half the cheque staged | 4.5 | Medium | 12-24 months, to the 2027 season and the licence test | S95 (unverified), S1 (unverified) |

### What is good, and what decides it

The pain is real and independently measured: hand-pick labour runs $21,056-23,949 an acre-season on the report's own yield and piece rate, and a robot at $2,714 an acre is 11-13% of that bill. The picker has the only labelled field dataset in the category — 94% pick rate on 212 rows, 75 paid robot-seasons, 110 robots contracted for 2027 at a $12,700 renewal price — and the two things that usually kill hardware start-ups, no customer and no evidence, are not the problem here. Four facts outweigh that. One robot-season loses $8,100 at the signed price, and the $33,000 build that would fix it is a single quote from a counterparty that is also noteholder, customer, board observer and investor. Bruising at 3.8% has already cost one grower and spends most of the USDA allowance before the fruit reaches a cooler. The licence falls non-exclusive below 100 robots on 2027-12-31, and the cash covenant is reached near 2027-03-10 if the close slips. Against that, the consensus that Orrin is the only open-field harvester above 90% and that a 2.1-season payback justifies the mark is not an edge: the price is 36.8x FY2025 revenue against a 2.3x listed peer median. [S119, S1, S95, S86]

The follow-up diligence is narrow and cheap: two independent manufacturer quotes for the v4, an independent cold-storage bruising trial, the note purchase agreement, the lender's consent, and a quality-of-earnings review of the last full year.

What does a fourth-generation robot cost to build at fleet volumes, quoted by a manufacturer that is not also the largest customer?

At the current build cost no price growers have signed makes a robot-season profitable, so the fleet consumes capital on every unit; at a lower cost the list price turns contribution positive and the business becomes financeable. Two competitive quotes settle it in weeks and decide between a capital-consuming lease book and a business that compounds.

1. Pass at $72M pre-money: at the signed $9,500 price and the $48,000 build, one robot-season loses $8,100, and the $12M ticket returns 1.04x on the plan's own probabilities — capital preservation, not a venture return (company-reported). [S1, S95]
2. The company is worth pursuing at a lower price: at a $50-58M pre-money with a 1.5x preference and half the cheque staged on two independent quotes at or below $33,000 and 200 robots in paid service, the same $100M exit returns about 1.5x on company-reported terms. [S95]
3. The binding constraints are physical and contractual, not commercial: bruising, coverage of 1.0-1.2 acres per 24 hours against a claimed 1.5, a licence cliff at 100 robots on 2027-12-31, and a California standard that still requires a human driver. [S1, S86, S126]

## 公司概览 Company Overview

Orrin Fieldworks's $72.0M pre-money is arithmetically coherent, but the issuer is not the entity that holds the grower contracts, the fleet and the equipment lien; the $12M should be committed only on verified entity, lien and licence conditions. It is a Delaware corporation with 38 staff, three hardware generations shipped by 2026-03, $1.9M FY2025 revenue and 75 paid robot-seasons in 2026 — all company-reported, unverified. The price works only on a share count the deck does not print: $72.0M ÷ 15,272,108 pre-money fully diluted shares = $4.7145, and $18.0M buys 3,818,008 shares, 20.0% of a $90.0M post. But 15,272,108 is not the "12,000,000 fully diluted total" beside it, which at $4.7145 is $56.6M. It absorbs the $7.77M note conversion and a 12% post-money pool; every derived figure needs rebuilding before a term sheet. No Delaware charter, California foreign-qualification record, UCC-1, Mexico Registro Público de Comercio entry, USPTO assignment record or registrar confirmation was retrieved; the section rests on four source IDs — S1 (deck), S10 (UC Davis cost study) and S27/S28 (peers) — and every table status means the deck is the sole support, so no structure, ownership or lien statement is diligence-grade and confidence is capped at company-reported [S1].

### The $72M sits below its own preference stack

The 1x non-participating preference ranks equally across Series A ($18.0M), Series A-1 ($7.77M) and Series Seed ($11.0M assumed from the 2023 round size, not stated in the deck): a $36.8M stack, 40.9% of the $90.0M post. Common receives nothing below $36.8M, and the preferred converts only above a $79.0M exit. At $4.7145 the Series A returns 1.0x at $79M and needs $180M for 2x, so the pre-money is best underwritten as an option struck at $79M, not a mark on the common. The structure is founder-friendly; the stack decides if a modest success reaches common. Company-reported, unverified [S1].

### What it sells, and to whom

Orrin sells a robot-season, not a robot. The customer is a strawberry grower and the budget owner holds the harvest-labour line: in the 2024 UC Davis Central Coast cost study, harvest costs $79,288 an acre against $22,264 of cultural costs, 70.4% of the $112,694 total cost per acre, so the machine targets most of the grower's cost base [S1, S10]. Growth comes from converting pilots into paid seasonal rentals: 14 pilot farms since 2024, two conversions in 2025, five paying growers in 2026, four of them contracted for 2027 (110 robots), plus 50 letters of intent. Revenue quality is thinner than the $3.2M ARR headline: $1.4M is contracted robot-seasons at the $12,700 renewal price, $1.2M is engineering services ending 2027-06-30, $0.6M is non-binding letters. The $8M ARR milestone is unreachable on the funded fleet: 360 robots at $12,700 is $4.6M, at the $16,500 list price $5.9M. Company-reported, unverified.

### Governance: five roles in one counterparty and an empty chair

The board is five seats — two common, one seed, one Series A, one independent agreed by both — but the independent seat is vacant, so the tie-breaker is unfilled and the chief executive chairs. Tallis Agricultural Machinery is at once a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year customer, the quoted manufacturer whose $33,000 unit cost underpins the $9.9M robot budget, a board observer and a $1.0M investor. The chief operating officer's wholly owned services company took $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to date under a contract approved by a board he sits on, and his 2014-2021 employer is the largest customer. Company-reported, unverified [S1]. Conditions before closing:

- An independent director at signing, agreed by the lead, chairing audit and compensation.
- Observer rights limited to non-confidential sessions.
- A second independent quote for the v4 bill of materials.
- Kestrel consent, a covenant waiver through the 2027 build, and Calder consent to affiliate operation and sublicensing.
- Founder reverse-vesting and a full-time chief financial officer by closing.

## 创始人与核心团队 Founding Team & Key Personnel

The team is built for the problem Orrin had in 2021, not the one it has in 2027. Dr. Imani Castellano, chief executive and chair, is a perception researcher with a robotics PhD, five years in a university field-robotics lab and eleven claimed patent filings; Teodor Vashti, chief operating officer, ran harvest operations for two large berry growers over twenty years. Neither has founded or sold a company, none of the five executives has built hardware at volume, and the co-founder who owned the technical roadmap left on 2023-08-31. Every degree, date, employer and patent count here is company-reported and unverified: no registrar, employer or patent-inventor record was retrievable, so the people-risk score is critical on unverified credentials, not medium [S1].

### The pairing fits two problems and misses the third

The combination matches the first two problems a picking robot has to solve — seeing ripe fruit, and being allowed onto a farm — and not the third, making 360 of them. Castellano invents and raises: the licensed families come out of her lab, the company holds five filings, and she is the face of the raise. Vashti sells and operates: five paying growers in 2026, four contracted for 2027, the two named ones taking 53% of the 75 paid robot-seasons, and the largest is the farm where he was harvest operations director from 2014 to 2021, contracted for 40 robots in 2027. That is commercial proof and its limit: the funnel is one man's twenty-year network, and the plan needs 250 more in a four-month window. Company-reported, unverified [S1].

### A CTO seat empty for 26 months

The co-founder and CTO, Dr. Soren Abernathy, left on 2023-08-31 and the role has been open for 26 months. He keeps 720,000 vested common shares — 6.0% before the round, 3.8% after — a permanent cap-table party without a reason to protect it. A patent-register search under the company's name on 2026-10-30 returned no Orrin assignee record and no inventor list for the two licensed families or five company filings; unpublished applications are not public for 18 months, so this is a gap, not a contradiction, but the deck's claim that he is a named inventor cannot be verified. The licensed families sit in the university's name, so an Orrin assignee search would miss them. No public footprint or new venture found. A 3.8% holder with unrestricted shares and the core perception work in his head is hireable by any competitor; California does not let the company restrain where he works. Company-reported, unverified [S1].

### The technical bet sits one level below the executive team

Dr. Mei Hollander joined as VP Engineering in 2024-02 with a PhD in mechanical engineering (2013) and eleven years at one robotics company, moving from manipulation engineer to gripper engineering manager — company-reported, unverified. That matches the bruising problem — 3.8% of berries damaged in the 2025 pilots, one Florida grower gone in 2026-06 — and not the problem that decides 2027: cutting the build from $48,000 to a $33,000 average while multiplying the fleet by 5.6. With no CTO above her, the hardest programme sits with one vice president hired 32 months ago, on an undisclosed equity package. Company-reported, unverified [S1].

### Selling 360 robots with one new sales leader

Dolores Achterberg joined as VP Sales in 2025-06 after twenty years at a crop-inputs company, ending as regional sales director for the West: sixteen months in robotics, unverified. The 2027 book is 110 robots contracted plus 50 under non-binding letters of intent, 31% of the 360-robot plan five months before the season, with two founder-sellers and one VP to close the gap. The risk is not product rejection; this industry buys late, the season opens in April in California and December in Florida, and a 360-unit build must be committed before the orders exist. No stage pipeline is shown. Company-reported, unverified [S1].

### What would settle it

Three records would turn biography into evidence; none was retrievable: degree checks through each registrar, patent-inventor records for the eleven claimed filings and the five company filings, and reference calls at the four prior employers. The peer record shows why the hires matter. Their first-three-year metrics could not be retrieved, so the comparison is one of outcomes, not like-for-like execution. Against the company's own history, the fleet went from 12 robots in 2024 to 64 in 2026, a 5.3x over two seasons, while the plan asks for 5.6x in one season and a one-third cost cut. People risk should therefore be priced: a CTO, a manufacturing leader and a retention grant for the VP Engineering are closing conditions, not intentions. The implication is that people risk is a condition precedent, not a diligence note. Company-reported, unverified [S1].

## 技术与产品 Technology & Product

The Picker has proved more than any published strawberry harvester and less than its own deck claims. The 94 percent pick rate is a genuine measurement with a stated denominator; the 1.5 acres per 24 hours does not survive arithmetic at a realistic ripe-fruit density; 3.8 percent bruising spends three quarters of the packer's damage allowance; and the patent position is a licensed perception stack, one gripper application whose claims were all rejected, and a PCT whose national-phase date is today [S1, S119].

### 5.6 seconds a berry buys about one acre of clean picking, not 1.5

Two arms at 5.6 seconds a berry place one berry every 2.8 seconds, so 20 working hours yield 25,714 berries at full uptime and 22,114 at the stated 86 percent uptime. The UC Davis Central Coast cost study models 9,000 trays an acre, each tray eight one-pound clamshells, which is 72,000 lb or 1.17-1.42 million berries an acre over a season. At the deck's own three-to-four-day pick interval over a seven-month season, about 60 passes, roughly 21,800 berries stand ripe on an acre at each pass. One robot therefore clears 1.0 acre a day at 86 percent uptime and 1.2 acres at full uptime, 20-33 percent below the claim. Picking 1.5 acres clean needs 32,700 berries, or 29.6 hours of running; holding 1.5 acres in 24 hours instead means picking 68 percent of the standing ripe crop, which reconciles with a 94 percent pick rate only if the interval shortens to 2.4 days. The claim is a drive-over capacity figure, not a picked-acre figure. Compared with Harvest CROO, the unit arithmetic is identical and the acreage eight times higher, so coverage follows capital per machine, not a better algorithm [S1, S27].

### Damage is most of the way to the grade limit before the fruit leaves the field

The bruising number matters more than the pick rate because it decides revenue. The U.S. No. 1 lot tolerance allows 10 percent of berries to fail the grade, of which at most 5 percent may show serious damage and 2 percent decay. A 3.8 percent bruise-or-puncture rate at picking consumes 76 percent of the serious-damage allowance and 38 percent of the defect budget, before field rots and the week in which a bruise expresses itself. Add 2.1 percent unripe picks and 5.9 percent of the fruit the robot touches is off-spec at the moment of picking, against a lot allowance the grower also spends on everything else. That is the mechanism behind the one grower that ended its pilot over bruising, and why a 94 percent pick rate coexists with a grower who did not renew [S1, S120].

**The picker's economics turn on damage, not pick rate: at 3.8 percent, one machine operation spends 76 percent of the USDA serious-damage allowance, and the company does not say whether it measured at pick or after cooling. [S1, S120]**

Packers work to a lot-level allowance for total defects, serious damage and decay rather than a per-machine one, and a bruise that appears after a week in the cooler is still the grower's loss.

## 市场与行业分析 Market & Industry Analysis

The US strawberry harvest is a $3.1-3.5B annual cost pool and hand-pick labour alone is worth $21,056-23,949 an acre-season, but the company's $310M obtainable market — a company estimate the deck does not source, unverified — is a slice of that cost pool, not a revenue line: at $16,500 a robot-season and one robot per 3.5 acres, all 50,000 US strawberry acres are worth $236M a year, and the 15% adoption assumed for 2031 is worth $35.4M. The addressable base is smaller than 50,000 open-field acres because tabletop production and mechanisation breeding can move acres to other machines, so the question is adoption speed, price per robot and the share Orrin keeps [S1, S136, S138].

**The $310M obtainable market is a slice of the harvest-cost pool, not a revenue forecast.** All 50,000 US acres at $16,500 and one robot per 3.5 acres are worth $236M; $310M needs 132% of the base. **One acre-season, three figures:** 9,000 trays (72,000 lb at 8 lb a tray), hand-pick labour of $21,056-23,949 and total harvest cost of $79,288; the robot fee is $2,714 an acre at $9,500 (11-13% of the wage bill) and $4,714 at $16,500 (20-22%). **The base is not all open field:** Cal Poly calls Santa Maria tabletop and hoop-house acreage "limited" without a figure, and Driscoll's is raising beds and breeding for mechanisation. Sources: S1, S80, S10, S136, S138.

The top-down series shows a stable crop, not a growing one. California planted 43,726 strawberry acres for 2026, up 2.0% from 42,885 in 2025, and produces 90% of the US crop; Florida is the other 10%. Prices did not follow volume: USDA Agricultural Marketing Service terminal prices averaged $23.05 a flat in 2026 to mid-June against $24.75 in 2025 and $24.67 in 2024, a 3.3% CAGR decline. A robot that saves labour sells into a crop growing 2.0% in acreage and shrinking in unit value, so growth must come from penetration, not the crop [S9, S8].

### One acre-season, three figures that reconcile
The bottom-up test starts from the cost the robot displaces: one acre-season is 9,000 trays (72,000 lb, the 8-lb flat of the UC budget), $21,056-23,949 of hand-pick labour and $79,288 of total harvest cost; hand-pick labour is 27-30% of that, and the rest — packing materials, supervision, hauling and cooling — is not what the robot displaces. The labour figure has two independent supports that agree: 1,280 picker-hours an acre-season (four picker-days a pass, company estimate, over 40 passes at eight hours) at the 2026 California adverse effect wage rates of $16.45 and $18.71 an hour is $21,056-23,949, and 9,000 trays at $1.75-2.25 a tray is $15,750-20,250 before an 18-34% payroll burden, the same range. There are 9,000 trays, not 1,125: reading a tray as eight flats understates the wage bill eight-fold, to $2,000-2,500. At $9,500 a robot-season over 3.5 acres Orrin charges $2,714 an acre, 11-13% of the hand-pick bill; at the $16,500 list, $4,714, or 20-22%. A 10% harvest-cost saving is worth $7,929 an acre, so the grower's payback survives the list price; what binds is quality and capital, not the size of the wage bill [S10, S12, S80, S1].

### The obtainable market fails its own arithmetic, and the base is smaller
The $310M figure, a company estimate, unverified, requires 18,788 robots, or 65,758 acres at one robot per 3.5 acres — 132% of the 50,000-acre US base; all US strawberry acreage at that density and price is $236M. At 15% adoption, 7,500 acres support 2,143 robots and $35.4M, so the 2031 revenue case is one-ninth of the stated obtainable market. The financial plan is ahead of the adoption slide: $12.9M of FY2028 RaaS revenue at $16,500 implies 782 robots, 2,737 acres and 5.5% of the base, not 2%. The base itself is not all open field: Cal Poly's Strawberry Center reports "limited strawberry acreage" under hoop houses in Santa Maria, with both in-ground and the newer tabletop systems using them, and no US tabletop acreage is published. Driscoll's, the largest berry marketer, is helping growers raise growing surfaces to waist height and will optimise breeding for mechanisation traits. A variety bred for a single destructive pass took processing tomatoes from 0.5% to 70% machine-harvested between 1961 and 1966; a berry breeder pursuing the same trait would move acres from selective picking to a once-over machine. Every 1,000 acres converted removes $4.7M of annual robot revenue at Orrin's density and list price, and a 20% shift of California's 43,726 acres would remove $41M (author calculations); neither conversion appears in the plan [S1, S12, S136, S138, S33].

### California and Florida are two different businesses
California's season runs seven months from April to October and Florida's from December to March, so a fleet working both is utilised for eleven months and a fleet working one is idle half the year. Open-field raised beds remain the norm; tabletop under high tunnels is a small but growing exception. California holds four of Orrin's five paying growers in 2026 and Florida one; four of the five have contracted 110 robots for 2027. Mexico is a competing supply source rather than a market: it supplies 20% of US terminal strawberry quotes and is the target of a 2026 trade case, while Orrin's only Mexican asset is a Guadalajara assembly subsidiary. Home, revenue and supplier markets are therefore US and Mexican; the capital and exit markets are US venture capital and US agricultural equipment, not Europe or Australia [S9, S13, S14].

### The shortage is real; the policy tailwind is not
The wage floor that sets the grower's alternative cost moved against Orrin before it moved for it. The Department of Labor's 2025-10-02 interim final rule — the wage-floor policy — replaced the Farm Labor Survey basis for the adverse effect wage rate; its 2026 rates were $16.45 and $18.71 an hour in California and $12.47 and $15.06 in Florida, below the rates they replaced, and on 2026-08-26 a California district court held the methodology unlawful and ordered a replacement, so a higher California rate is more likely than not in 2027. The risk cuts both ways: a lower Florida floor lengthens payback, a California reversal shortens it. H-2A certifications reached 398,258 in FY2025, 13,358 more than FY2024: the guest-worker programme has expanded every year and is the main reason the shortage has not become a permanent 10-15% crop loss. Independent evidence for the deck's 10-15% loss figure, a company estimate that remains unverified, is episodic: June 2025 enforcement in Ventura County left up to 70% of workers absent. The mechanisation base rate is unforgiving — processing tomatoes reached 70% only after UC bred a machine-harvestable variety and growers moved to a single destructive pass, a system change fresh-market strawberries have not made. Underwrite 2-5% penetration by 2028 rather than 2% rising to 15%. Three diligence questions remain: the 40 passes and 3.5-acre density behind the robot count; the final 2027 California and Florida rates after the court order; and the share of California acreage in tabletop [S15, S18, S33, S80, S117].

## 竞争格局 Competitive Landscape

Orrin is not alone. Harvest CROO Robotics announced on 2025-04-24 that its B8 harvester matched human picking rates in a commercial operation at Duette, Florida — an open-field claim the deck's "only above 90%" statement does not acknowledge. The claim is company-issued and unverified, but Driscoll's has invested in Harvest CROO and Agrobot and is talking to six startups. The hand crew, harvest-aid platform and 2025 exits discipline Orrin's price more than any rival [S27, S28, S138].

**The field is thinner than the narrative implies, and not empty.** Harvest CROO claimed human-parity open-field picking in Florida in April 2025 (company claim, unverified); Advanced Farm closed in 2025; Tortuga's IP and team went to Oishii; Tallis could build the platform. **Commercial proof is concentrated:** five paying growers in 2026, four of which contracted 110 robots for 2027. Sources: S27, S28, S34, S1.

The field consolidated in 2025. Advanced Farm, which had reached named California growers, ceased operations; Tortuga sold its IP, assets and team to Oishii. No public shares exist; the proxy is paid robot-seasons — Orrin's 75 in 2026 equal 262 acres at one robot per 3.5 acres, 0.5% of the 50,000-acre base — so Orrin is the largest disclosed paid base, not a demonstrated leader [S28, S34, S1].

### The 2021 cohort failed on unit economics, not on picking
Abundant Robotics shut down in 2021 after commercial apple trials; Root AI, an indoor tomato picker, sold to AppHarvest for $60 million in April 2021; Traptic, a strawberry picker, was acquired in 2022 (reported). The pattern is a hardware business whose unit cost falls only with volume while growers buy on a one-season payback. All three causes — unit cost, field reliability and the next financing round — apply to Orrin: the v3 robot costs $48,000, its target payback is 2.1 seasons, and it had $3.7M of cash against $410,000 monthly net burn at 2026-09-30 [S29, S32].

### The grower's harvest budget has cheaper bidders than a robot
The robot competes with a hand crew paid by output, not with other robots. A picker earns $1.75-2.25 a tray at 8-12 trays an hour; hand-pick labour is $21,056-23,949 an acre-season and a field is picked 40-50 times. Agrobot's solar platform carries pickers and claims a 30-40% labour saving — unverified, but it captures part of the saving with no autonomy or bruising risk. Equipment makers are the other bidder: a picking arm on an existing platform is cheaper than a fleet. Orrin charges $2,714 an acre at $9,500 and $4,714 at the $16,500 list, 11-22% of the hand-pick bill; the headroom is real, but a lower-cost platform could capture the easy half [S12, S77].

### Who is most dangerous, and what is the wedge
Harvest CROO is the most dangerous direct competitor: same open-field architecture and RaaS model, 13 patents and a Florida commercial claim. Its weaknesses are a December-March season, no published performance data and no California service network, where Orrin has five paying growers in 2026, four of which contracted 110 robots for 2027. Orrin's wedge is night operation, direct clamshell packing, a 3.8% bruising rate on its test rows and the COO's California grower relationships: a service and quality advantage in one geography, not a technology monopoly. Waseda University's Sugano Lab with Maekawa runs a rail-mounted night harvester under elevated beds; Nanjing Agricultural University's Wang Xiaochan team demonstrated a tracked robot at 20 seconds a berry and 84% grasp success; Washington State University has built a hidden-fruit picker — all research, no commercial open-field deployment and no published price, so none sets a ceiling on the $16,500 list today, though the perception stack is being solved in public and erodes the licensed families' value when the Calder licence becomes non-exclusive on 2027-12-31 [S30, S1, S139, S135, S137, S134].

| Tabletop / high-tunnel harvest | Not addressed: open-field platform only | Manual tabletop crews | Greenhouse robot vendors | Waseda/Maekawa rail harvester (research) | Once-over machine-harvest varieties | S136, S138, S139 |

### The price is the tell, and the marketer co-signs
Orrin raised its price from $9,500 per robot-season on 2025-26 contracts to a $16,500 list for 2027, a 73.7% increase. The deck's own disclosure has the counter-evidence: Grower E in Plant City ended its pilot over fruit bruising, and 53% of 2026 robot-seasons sit with two named growers; four of the five paying growers nevertheless contracted 110 robots for 2027. If Harvest CROO's claim holds, the $16,500 list converges on displaced labour; if the 3.8% bruising holds at retail, it can keep pricing up. The buyer is not only the grower: Orrin Fleet Services LLC signs the season contract, but the grower cannot commit fruit its marketer will not sell, and Driscoll's — the largest US berry marketer — is helping growers raise beds, will optimise breeding for mechanisation and has invested in two harvesting-robot companies. The deck discloses no marketer or packer sign-off on machine-picked fruit and no pilot decision dates; the 2027 contracts for 110 robots and two letters of intent for 50 robots would settle who accepted what and when. Two substitutes shrink the acres rather than bid: tabletop and high-tunnel production, and a once-over variety of the kind that took processing tomatoes from 0.5% to 70% in five years. Tallis is the other exposure: contract manufacturer, noteholder, board observer and investor with the BOM and the cost quote. Diligence: is bruising measured against a retailer spec or only test rows; what prevents Tallis competing; and what share of California acreage is tabletop [S1, S28, S136, S138, S33].

## 商业模式 Business Model

On the company's unverified figures, the signed $9,500 price loses $8,100 on every robot-season after depreciation, and even the 2027 contracted price of $12,700 leaves the target-build v4 $650 short, so the case rests on a $16,500 list price no grower has signed and a $31,000 build not yet built. The grower pays Orrin Fleet Services LLC per robot per season — about seven months in California and four in Florida — and Orrin owns, maintains and insures the fleet; the term is one season and no multi-year contract is disclosed. Five growers paid in 2026; four contracted 110 robot-seasons for 2027 at a $12,700 average, and the fifth is in discussion. FY2025 revenue of $1.9M is rental $0.38M (20.0%), paid pilots $0.27M (14.2%), related-party engineering services $0.95M (50.0%) and grants $0.30M (15.8%); FY2026E rental is $0.71M of $2.6M (27.3%), so 80% of FY2025 revenue was one-off, grant-funded or related-party. No new grower has signed for 2027; the only new-logo demand is two non-binding letters for 50 robots from eight pilot farms. Same-store robots rise 64 to 110 (+71.9%) at a price 33.7% higher: real demand from four accounts, none a new logo [S1].

The commercial cycle is annual. First paid deployment follows the first field trial by one season in every converted account: 2024 pilots became 2025 seasons at two growers, 2025 pilots became 2026 seasons at two more, and the 2024-25 Florida pilot became a paid 2025-26 season; the 2027 contracts were signed by 2026-09-30, about six months before the April season. The buying unit includes the marketer or packer, not only the grower: the robot packs straight into retail clamshells, so whoever sells or packs the fruit must accept machine-picked berries, and the 3.8% bruising that ended Grower E's pilot shows acceptance can be lost after a field trial. Whether a marketer's acceptance is a contract condition, and who signs — owner, VP of growing or procurement — is not disclosed; executed contracts and the packer's fruit specification would settle both. Orrin bears most of the pilot cost; grower payments appear only in the paid-pilot line ($0.27M FY2025, $0.34M FY2026E). Against nine 2025 test farms, about $30,000 paid a pilot farm against $53,000-$70,000 of direct cost leaves $23,000-$40,000 unrecovered per pilot and $64,000-$113,000 per converted grower at five of 14. Non-renewals are visible: Grower B cut its paid fleet from 22 robots in 2025 to 14 in 2026 (-36%) before contracting 20 for 2027; Grower D paid for 11 robots in 2025-26 and is only "in discussion" for 2027; Grower E ended its pilot over fruit bruising and has no 2027 contract. No lapsed account is disclosed buying a competing robot, so hand crews remain the substitute. The contract is one season with no disclosed cancellation, deposit or uptime terms. Standard RaaS terms run one to five years with uptime service levels and early-termination fees; a one-season contract gives the grower an annual option and Orrin the residual value, so the book is 110 options, not a backlog (company-reported, unverified) [S1, S140].

|---|---|---|---|
| Price per robot-season | 9,500 | 100.0 | S1 (unverified) |
| Field service and remote supervision | (3,100) | 32.6 | S1 (unverified) |
| Transport, insurance, consumables | (2,500) | 26.3 | S1 (unverified) |
| Gross profit as reported | 3,900 | 41.1 | S1 (unverified) |
| Fleet depreciation ($48,000 / 4 seasons) | (12,000) | 126.3 | S1 (unverified), calc |

The gross margin of 41.1% is a policy artefact: $12,000 of depreciation sits in operating expense, not cost of revenue, so $3,900 of gross profit becomes a contribution margin of -85.3%, or -$8,100, once the robot is charged to the season. Depreciation and debt service are two views of one asset and must not be added: cash is +$1,447 if the $1.6M facility is interest-only (11.5%, $2,453 a season) and -$3,051 if it amortises over four years ($6,951 a season). United Rentals earned a 38.0% rental gross margin in FY2025 after $2,670M of fleet depreciation, 19.3% of rental revenue; Orrin's -85.3% becomes -6.7% at list with the v3 and +19.1% only with both list and a $31,000 v4 [S21]. The claimed 2.1-season payback uses a $31,000 build, the $16,500 list price and a $1,750 service cost, none signed at once, and drops the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line; putting that back gives 2.53 seasons. At the signed $9,500 and the reported $5,600 cost, payback on the $48,000 v3 is 12.31 seasons, or 10.5 years at the 1.17 seasons per robot the fleet ran in 2026. At the $31,000 build the signed price pays back in 7.95 seasons; at $12,700 it is 4.37, longer than the asset lasts (company-reported, unverified) [S1, S21].

The economics are inverted: gross margin rises as capital moves into opex, while the cash to build each robot leaves before the season.

The fleet ran 75 paid robot-seasons on 64 robots in 2026, 1.17 of a physical maximum of two, since the two state seasons cover eleven months. At the signed price it needs 3.08 seasons per robot-year to cover depreciation, 154% of the maximum; at $12,700 it needs 1.69 (85%); at $16,500 with the v3 it needs 1.10. Running a robot twice a year doubles revenue and consumes its life twice as fast, so utilisation spreads overhead but cannot lower the per-season capital charge. One technician per eight robots at the UC Davis 2024 field-labour rate of $24.42 an hour over 213 days costs $5,201 per robot-season ($6,305 at the $29.60 operator rate), against $3,100 reported; at 360 robots, 45 technicians cost $1.87M against $1.12M implied by the $3,100 line, so service cost is linear and understated. On $6,305 gross profit at the signed price is $695, 7.3%, before depreciation. At 3.5 acres a robot the signed price is $2,714 an acre and the list $4,714, 11.3-12.9% and 19.7-22.4% of hand-pick labour of $21,056-23,949 an acre-season: one pass over an acre costs $526-599 (8 hours at the $16.45-18.71 Level I-II adverse effect wage rate over a quarter acre) and a season is 40 passes, which on 9,000 trays is $2.34-2.66 a tray all-in against a $1.75-2.25 piece rate plus burden. Western Growers' survey requires a one-to-two-year payback; at 1.17 seasons a year the 2.84-season payback is 2.4 years, and the signed-price payback is 10.5 (company-reported, unverified deck figures; external benchmarks) [S1, S10, S80, S141].

The counter-evidence is that the robot is priced at 11-13% of hand-pick labour at the signed price and 20-22% at list, so a working unit could charge more; but two better-capitalised peers did not get there. Tortuga deployed 150 harvesting robots and about $50M over eight years before selling its IP and team to Oishii in 2025-03; FarmWise raised $65M, ran Titan as a service, moved Vulcan to dealer sales and wound down, acquired by Taylor Farms in 2025-04. Orrin's $320,313 per robot in service is essentially Tortuga's $333,000. The unit turns positive only with a build at or below $31,000 and a price at or above $13,350, and the 2027 list of $16,500 is the only price that clears both; the 110 signed at $12,700 do not. For an investor, the signed book is $1.4M of 2027 rental; the $16,500 list and $31,000 v4 must be proven before paying for fleet capex. Conditions: executed contracts with cancellation and deposit terms, an independent v4 bill of materials, a service-cost build at 1:8 and a grower-validated bruising tolerance. The arithmetic is high confidence; the pilot-cost estimate is medium; open questions are loan amortisation, the Florida price and marketer acceptance (company-reported, unverified) [S1, S93, S100, S116].

**At the signed price, one robot-season does not cover its own depreciation, so every additional season sold at that price consumes capital.**

The deck (company-reported, unverified) reports price $9,500, field service $3,100, transport/insurance/consumables $2,500, gross profit $3,900 and a $48,000 v3 build depreciated over four seasons in operating expense; the $1.6M facility carries 11.5% interest and the fleet ran 75 robot-seasons on 64 robots in 2026. These produce the -$8,100 contribution, 12.31-season payback and 3.08-season breakeven. Source S1.

## 财务分析 Financial Analysis

On the company's unverified figures, the $18M is sized to the 2027 robot budget but not to 2028, and the minimum $12M funds only 200 robots; run on its own use of funds, the $12M case holds the $1.5M covenant through 2027 and crosses it in the 2028 build, and most reported ARR is not recurring rental. The company supplies FY2023-FY2028P income statements but no balance sheet, cash flow or auditor. Revenue compounds at 90.9% a year from FY2025 to FY2028P, cumulative net losses reach $32.0M, operating expenses are 265% of revenue in FY2026E, and total gross margin is 51.8% in FY2027 before 60.6% in FY2028, so "60%+ at scale" is a 2028 event. Revenue quality is the larger problem: 80% of FY2025 revenue was one-off pilots, related-party engineering or grants, so the base the plan multiplies is a rental line of $0.38M [S1].

The floor is crossed in Q1 2028, when the first $1.885M of the 2028 build is spent — about 57 robots; the $12M case needs 518 more robots and $17.1M to reach the 2028 plan's 782, so the 2028 fleet is unfunded (unverified) [S1].

The $18M case follows the same lines with $9.9M of capex for 300 robots, 364 in service against 360 planned, and the same $4.69M of burn: $6.085M at 2027-12-31, $4.585M above the floor, but still $9.3M short of the $13.93M 2028 build, so the full round also needs a Series B. Neither path carries working capital: grower payment terms are not disclosed, and the full $4.6M 2027 season unpaid at year-end would leave the $12M case at -$1.2M, $2.7M below the floor. A close delayed past 2027-03-10 puts opening cash at $1.513M or less, below the floor before the money arrives (unverified) [S1].

The data room would settle revenue recognition, grower arrears and payment terms, the loan's amortisation and covenant test, v3 impairment from the v4 launch, and the company's own use-of-funds schedule for a $12M close; until then the figures are company-reported and unverified. Only list price with a build at or below $36,000 produces positive contribution; price is the bigger swing, but build cost is the gate because no price makes the v3 work. The full round still needs a Series B before 2028; the minimum funds 2027 only. The counter-evidence is that $18M funds 2027 with $6.085M left, the 110 seasons are contracted and the $0.9M undrawn facility could bridge the minimum case; none of that closes the 2028 capex gap [S1, S37].

### The disclosed private marks sit below $72M

Harvest CROO has raised $10M-$28.5M depending on the aggregator, with no disclosed valuation; Advanced Farm raised a $25M Series B in September 2021, ceased operations in July 2025 and sold its IP and team to CNH for undisclosed terms; Tortuga deployed $50M over eight years and 150 robots and sold its IP and team to Oishii in 2025-03 for undisclosed terms; Tevel raised $20M in 2021 and carries a reported $63M secondary value. Carbon Robotics raised $70M in October 2024 with no disclosed valuation, and Monarch raised $133M at more than $500M in July 2024 before laying off almost all staff. The only disclosed $100M+ ag-robotics exits are Deere's purchases of Blue River ($305M) and Bear Flag ($250M), both autonomy platforms. Orrin's $90M post is above every disclosed harvesting-robot mark and near Blue River's 2015 $87M post-money, eleven years earlier. [S105, S28, S94, S144]

### A $12M close improves the price and weakens the plan, while the preference delays the upside

The $18M target has only $4.0M committed and a $12M minimum (company-provided, unverified). At $12M the post-money is $84M, the lead owns 14.29% and the preference stack falls to $30.77M; the 2027 plan spends $9.9M of the $18M on 300 robots at a $33,000 average, so $12M funds about 200 robots, the 360-robot and $8M ARR milestones slip and a 2028 down round becomes the base case. At $16M — the lead's $12M plus the $4.0M committed — the post-money is $88M and the lead owns 13.64%. The company has $3.7M of cash and a $410,000 monthly burn, nine months of runway to June 2027, so the close must land in Q1 2027 to order robots for the 2027 season. On the full round the 1x preference returns the $12M in full at $40M, $60M and $90M; only above $90M does the lead participate — $20.0M at $150M (1.7x), $33.3M at $250M (2.8x) — while common and options receive $1.6M at $40M, $21.6M at $60M and $47.1M at $90M after the $1.6M debt. To return 3x in five years the company must be worth $270M at exit, which at a 3-5x revenue multiple requires $54-90M of revenue — four to seven times the 2028 plan. The price is defensible only if the 2027 milestones are met and a strategic buyer pays above the listed peer multiples; the diligence questions are the note schedule and seed charter, the 2027 order book and deposits, the option-pool refresh policy, and the source of the $6M of unfilled Series A. [S95]

## 发展方向与战略 Development Strategy

The plan does not add up on its own numbers, which are company-stated and unverified. At the current $48,000 build even the 2027 list price leaves each robot-season $1,100 short over a four-season life, the v4 must land below $28,400 to earn its keep at the $12,700 renewal price, the company's own FY2027 revenue projection implies an average price of $12,778 rather than the $16,500 list, and a 5.6-times fleet increase by April 2027 rests on one outsourced build quote and a $14M gap in a round that has not closed [S1].

### The price rise is a solvency requirement, not a margin story

At $5,600 a season of reported, unverified field service, transport, insurance and consumables, a robot priced at the $12,700 renewal average can cost at most $28,400 and still repay itself over four seasons; the v4 budget is $33,000. Priced at the $16,500 list it can cost $43,600 and still repay, which the $48,000 v3 does not. The gap is not theoretical: on the reported costs each robot-season at the renewal price loses $4,900, so a 360-robot fleet at the 2027 revenue line of $4.6M loses $1.76M a season before a dollar of overhead, and even the $33,000 v4 turns positive only if service cost also falls to the $1,750 target. Depreciation sits in operating expenses rather than cost of revenue, so the reported 52 percent gross margin for 2027 excludes $3.24M of hardware consumption on a $4.6M revenue line, alongside $2.02M of service cost, against total gross profit of $2.9M. The payback figure that carries the story uses the best case at every input: at a $31,000 build, the $16,500 list price and a $1,750 service cost, 2.1 seasons is right, but at the $5,600 the company reports, unverified, for 2026, payback stretches to 2.8 seasons at that build and 4.4 seasons at today's $48,000, longer than the four-season life the same page assumes. The gap between $1,750 and $5,600 is $3,850 a robot-season, $1.386M across 360 robots, and no cost bridge is disclosed for it [S1].

### A price that is too low to be replacing a hand crew

The pricing question runs the other way from the usual one. At $9,500 for the 3.5 acres a robot serves, a grower pays $2,714 an acre a season; the 2027 list is $4,714 an acre. The California Strawberry Commission puts the cost to cultivate and harvest strawberries at an average $87,000 an acre, $15.34 a tray, rising to $17.73 a tray in 2023, so Orrin's asking price is between 3 and 5 percent of the total cost of the crop [S1, S121]. A machine that replaced the hand crew over 3.5 acres would be worth several times that, and five growers buying 75 robot-seasons would not have left it on the table. Either the robot harvests a small fraction of the fruit on the acres it drives, or the price was set to buy pilots and the 2027 increase is the first real test of willingness to pay. Grower B cutting from 22 robots to 14 and Grower E exiting over bruising say the test is live; the two letters of intent for 50 robots are not contracts.

### Manufacturing risk sits with one supplier that is also a customer, a creditor and an investor

The build plan is 300 robots for $9.9M, 55 percent of the round, at an average $33,000 on a design that has never been manufactured. That is a 31 percent cut from the $48,000 v3 on a single quote from Tallis Agricultural Machinery dated 2026-08, a counterparty that is simultaneously a $2.5M noteholder, the $1.2M-a-year engineering-services customer, the quoted contract manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor in this round. Assembly sits in Guadalajara into a market where a Section 232 investigation into imported robotics and industrial machinery opened in September 2025 and a related proclamation followed on 2026-10-28; USMCA-qualifying goods enter at zero and non-qualifying at 10 percent, which on a $33,000 robot is $3,300 a unit, $990,000 across 300 units and 72 percent of the $4,600 of unit headroom between the v4 budget and break-even [S1, S87, S88, S89].

### Peers that carried the asset did not survive it

RaaS makes Orrin the lessor: at 64 robots it carries $3.07M of fleet on its balance sheet, at 360 $17.28M at the v3 build or $11.88M at the v4 budget, funded by $18M of equity and a $2.5M secured facility. Five of six comparable companies did not hold that position. Advanced Farm raised a $25M Series B in 2021, ceased operations in July 2025 and sold its IP to CNH; Tortuga moved to a per-kilogram service and sold its IP and engineering team to Oishii in March 2025; Monarch raised a $133M Series C at a reported valuation above $500M in 2024, cut staff, and had its assets bought by Caterpillar in April 2026 after failing to pivot to software services; Abundant Robotics shut down in 2021; FarmWise moved from a per-acre Titan service to selling through Vulcan dealers. Carbon Robotics, which sells machines and raised a $70M Series D, is the exception. The same arithmetic that makes RaaS hard for Orrin is why growers like it, and the base rate says the model is financeable only if the fleet turns fast: 75 paid robot-seasons from 5 growers in 2026 against 360 planned in 2027, with 53 percent of 2026 seasons in two named customers, one of them the chief operating officer's former employer [S1, S28, S93, S97, S109, S116, S122].

### What must be true in twelve months

Three things. The round closes by 2026-12-15 so that build slots and deposits are in place for an April 2027 season; the v4 reaches $33,000 or less on a second and third quote, because at $48,000 the fleet consumes its own gross profit; and at least one grower renews at or near the $16,500 list after a season with an independently measured pick rate and damage rate. The signposts are dated and checkable: a signed 2027 contract at list price, a second contract-manufacturing quote, the v4 first-article build date, and whether the 100-robot licence test is met by robots in commercial service rather than robots built. Against $3.7M of cash, $410,000 of monthly net burn and a $1.5M cash covenant, usable runway is 5.4 months; a close in January 2027 makes 360 robots impossible and puts the licence cliff at risk [S1, S91].

Two limitations bound this judgement. The v4 unit cost is a single unverified quote and the service-cost target has no disclosed bridge from the reported figure, so the margin case cannot be tested from outside; and the public record returns no federal award to the company, which contradicts the SBIR revenue line in the plan.

## 风险评估 Risk Assessment

Orrin has a real cost pool and a broken price: every robot-season it has sold loses $8,100 after depreciation at the $9,500 growers signed, the $33,000 v4 that would fix it is quoted by a counterparty that is also customer, noteholder and investor, and the California standard governing the fleet requires a human driver. The mechanism is a lessor whose build cost exceeds the value of its price: equity is consumed on every unit and the preference decides who absorbs it. The risk is that the $12M is subordinated before it is at risk. Company figures are unverified. [S1, S95]

### The 1.0x floor sits at $40M, not $25M

| $40M | 0.96x | 0.68x | 0.69x | 0.30x | S95 (unverified), calc |

The $36.77M preference is described in the deck, not the documents, and ranks behind $1.6M of secured fleet debt; net of debt and 8% costs the $12M is whole only at a $41.6M enterprise value — $39.4M at the likely $16M close, where the stack is $34.77M — and at $25M it returns 0.59x, which means the bear case must be priced off net proceeds. Down rounds were 11.4% of Carta's Q1 2026 rounds and 12.1% of Cooley's Q2 2026 deals, and new money asks for seniority or pay-to-play; the lead then funds pro rata or converts. With 82 of the plan's own probability points missing the 2027 plan, a 2028 down round is more likely than not at 45-55%, with 30-40% on senior or pay-to-play terms. A $15M purchase of patents, licence and team — the CNH and Oishii structure — pays $13.2M after costs and returns 0.36x; through the lender's collateral, nil. [S95, S123]

### The plan multiplies three numbers the deck does not have

The v4 misses $36,000 with a 55% probability, and FY2027 revenue of $4.6M is 360 robots at $12,778, but 110 are contracted ($1.4M, company-reported) and 250 must be signed in four months by two founders and one vice president hired in June 2025. At 250 robots revenue is $3.18M, and depreciation on 64 v3 and 186 v4 units is $2.30M against $1.78M of gross profit before it: -$0.53M, worse than the plan's -$0.31M, because field service does not shrink with the fleet. The 51.8% FY2027 margin excludes $3.21M of depreciation; with it the year is -5.5%, and the 2026 41% is rental-only. The 2028 plan needs 782 robots and $13.93M of unplanned capex. A close on 2027-02-15 arrives with $1.9M against a $1.5M floor: three weeks of headroom, a January waiver request and the only likely bridge from the counterparty already owed $2.5M — so the position becomes uninvestable at the first waiver request, not the first missed number. The build compounds it: 300 units of an unbuilt design ordered in February cannot reach an April season, so 2027 runs on 64 v3 robots and a partial build, revenue lands at $0.8-1.8M, the licence test fails below 100 robots on 2027-12-31, and the 2028 raise happens without exclusivity. A six-month delay does not slow this model; it ends the 2027 season. [S1]

### One counterparty, five roles

Tallis Agricultural Machinery holds $2.5M of the $7.77M notes (32.2%), commits $1.0M to this round, buys $1.2M a year of engineering (46% of FY2026E revenue), sits as board observer, and supplies the $33,000 quote behind 300 units and $9.9M of orders (company-reported). One counterparty touches $14.6M of the round and supplies the number that decides viability. A 10% error is $3,300 a unit and $825 a season of depreciation, taking contribution at $12,700 from -$1,150 to -$1,975; at $44,000 the $16,500 list price stops covering depreciation. The chief operating officer's own services company took $310,000 in 2025-2026, about two-thirds of the season's field-service line, on a contract approved by a board he sits on; at a 25% premium the leakage is $62,000. With the independent seat vacant, Meridian cannot carry a related-party resolution alone. The quote is an offer, not evidence: $50-58M with two independent quotes, not $72M. [S1, S95]

### The rule that actually breaks the model

California alone prohibits autonomous agricultural equipment, through Cal/OSHA standards requiring a human driver in agricultural workplaces; the fix died when AB 187 passed on 2026-08-31, and the Standards Board's advisory committee first meets on 2026-12-01, so no rule can change before the 2027 season. Both readings are fatal: if a technician satisfies the standard, the 1:8 ratio is the exposure and one technician a machine puts field service above the price of a season; if the fleet sits outside it, one citation ends a season that is all of the 2026 revenue. The probability of a material restriction or enforcement action in 2027 is 20% to 25%, with -70% to -90% of equity value. The tariff is likelier and less fatal: the 2026-10-28 proclamation found a threat, imposed nothing and set a Commerce-USTR report within 180 days — 2027-04-26, six days before the season — and a 25% duty is $8,250 a robot, $2.48M on 300 and a 75-robot smaller fleet at 30-35%. Non-USMCA origin at 10% costs $3,300 a robot, 85% of gross profit, with origin undocumented at 40%; Bayh-Dole US manufacture would cost $1,500-3,000 a robot to reshore if a licensed family was federally funded, at 30-40%. The wage floor helps at 60-70% odds but cannot fix bruising. [S126, S124, S88, S89, S85]

### Absence is a finding, not proof

No registry entry, no federal award against the grant the deck describes, no granted patent and no auditor's opinion: the inference is not misrepresentation but that every fact the decision turns on is management representation. Absence proves less than it seems: registries sit behind paywalls, applications stay unpublished for eighteen months, subawards appear on no federal site. It proves enough — the money would be wired on unverified facts, a condition-precedent problem before a price problem.

**The model-breaker is the California equipment prohibition, not the tariff.** California alone bars autonomous agricultural equipment, the fix died on 2026-08-31, and the committee does not sit until 2026-12-01. Both readings end the investment: one technician a machine puts field service above the price of a season, and a citation stops the only revenue line. [S126, S124]

On the plan's own probabilities the position returns about its capital over five years once the bear case is repriced to these structures — preservation at best, negative after fees and time. No price makes this a venture return while the v4 is unbuilt and contribution is negative at every signed price; the fix is evidence, and only a staged term sheet with two quotes, the licence warranty, the lender's consent and a higher preference buys it.

## 投资潜力与投资逻辑 Investment Potential & Thesis

Orrin has found a real harvest bill — $21,056-23,949 an acre-season of hand-pick labour — and built a picker whose own measurements are credible, but at the $9,500 price growers signed and the single-quoted $33,000 build cost (company-reported, unverified) every robot-season loses $8,100 after depreciation, so $72M pre-money prices a 2028 plan the company cannot fund and an outcome that returns capital at best. [S1, S95]

### The need is real; the fee is not the obstacle

Hand-pick labour is $21,056-23,949 an acre-season on 9,000 trays at a $1.75-2.25 piece rate plus burden. At $9,500 a robot-season across 3.5 acres, Orrin charges $2,714 an acre, 11-13% of the hand-pick bill, so affordability does not explain why only 110 robots are contracted for 2027. Two things do. The machine captures only the picking step, and its damage rate consumes the saving: 3.8% bruising spends 76% of the USDA 5% serious-damage allowance before the fruit reaches a cooler, and one point of culled fruit at 9,000 trays an acre and $11 a tray is $990 an acre, 36% of the annual fee. And the grower's alternative cost fell in 2026: the skill-based wage floor cut California's entry-level rate to $16.45 from $19.97 and Florida's to $12.47 from $16.23, making the deck's urgency a 2024 story sold in 2026. [S119, S80]

### The machine has proved more than any published rival and less than the deck

Ninety-four per cent on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms is measured with a stated denominator, and 75 paid robot-seasons is the only labelled field dataset in the category; the seller chose the rows, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%. Two arms at 5.6 seconds a berry over 20 hours at 86% uptime give 22,114 berries, or 1.0-1.2 acres in 24 hours at realistic fruit density, not 1.5. The durable asset is fleet data and service density in two California valleys, not patents: all five own filings are ungranted, the gripper application had every claim rejected with a response filed in 2026-05, and the two perception families are licensed and fall non-exclusive below 100 robots in paid service on 2027-12-31. [S1, S86]

### Consensus is the pain and the payback; our difference is what pays for it

The consensus is that Orrin is the only open-field strawberry harvester above 90%, that a 2.1-season payback follows and that 52-61% gross margins at scale justify $72M. All three are company constructions, unverified. The payback uses a $31,000 build, the $16,500 list and a $1,750 service cost, none signed, and the margins precede $3.21M and $6.45M of depreciation charged below the gross line; after it, FY2027 is -5.5%. The disagreement is not whether the picker works but the cash the lease book produces at $9,500 and a build cost no independent party has quoted; at that pair the answer is -$8,100 a season. [S1, S95]

### The sector's best outcome is a four-times return, and it was not a fleet

Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017, four times its last private post-money, buying perception for its sprayer line, not a fleet. Bear Flag sold to Deere for $250M, Tortuga and Advanced Farm sold IP and teams at undisclosed prices, and Monarch Tractor shut down in April 2026 after $133M raised. Orrin's $90M post-money needs a $270M exit to return 3x, above the sector's best recorded outcome. [S128, S131, S127, S130]

The probability-weighted return is 1.04x on company-reported inputs, unverified — 18% at 2.2x, 40% at 1.0x, 42% at 0.59x — capital preservation over five years, not a venture return; the Pass rests on the 1.0x floor at a $39.4-41.6M exit, not on the mean. The bull needs build, price, damage, licence and calendar together; the bear needs one of five failures. The $36.77M stack is one deck sentence and no document: the 1.04x and the rating assume it ranks 1x, non-participating and equal, and a $39.27M stack if the $2.5M of SAFEs convert would lower the floor further. Above the stack the preference and the as-converted share converge, so the premium is worth its face in the base case. The evidence needs to improve less than the price: independent v4 quotes and a note agreement on equal rank would reprice the same asset.

### The analogs that teach the rule

The exit pays for the perception asset or the team, not the lease book: a buyer prices the dataset and the grower relationships and treats a leased fleet as a liability. Because the fee sits below the cost of the asset, each additional robot moves value from equity to the grower, so growth enlarges the loss; the preference then decides whether that loss lands on the founder, the noteholder or this fund. For Meridian the implication is to decline at this mark and keep the diligence warm: both documents are cheap and would reprice the same asset.

## 退出策略分析 Exit Strategy Analysis

A $90M post-money entry into Orrin has no $100M+ precedent in strawberry harvesting: the two $100M+ ag-robotics exits were Deere's purchases of autonomy platforms Blue River ($305M) and Bear Flag ($250M), while harvesting peers sold IP and teams for undisclosed amounts or shut down. The realistic exit is a 2029-2031 trade sale to Deere, CNH or Kubota at $100-250M, which returns the $12M lead 1.0-2.2x after dilution and 1.04x probability-weighted — capital returned, not a venture return. [S98, S96]

### Who buys, what they buy, and when

Deere paid $305M for Blue River and $250M for Bear Flag and would buy the perception model, gripper IP and grower relationships that extend See & Spray into berries. CNH owns Raven ($2.1B) and the Advanced Farm IP and team (2025) and would buy a second harvesting technology and the California/Florida grower base. Kubota owns AgJunction ($73M) and has invested in Tevel and Advanced Farm; it would buy harvesting technology for Japan and Asia. AGCO has PTx Trimble ($2.35B EV) but little need for a berry fleet. A berry marketer such as Driscoll's, California Giant or Naturipe would buy harvest security and grower data, not equipment. The OEMs do not need Orrin's 64-robot fleet, a liability unless the buyer wants the service contracts. [S96, S98, S99, S97, S104, S107, S102, S101]

| Strategic OEM | CNH Industrial | Harvesting technology and team; grower base | 2028-2030 | Medium | S99, S97 |
| Strategic OEM | Kubota | Fruit-harvesting technology for Japan and Asia | 2028-2030 | Medium-low | S104, S107, S102 |
| Precision-ag OEM | AGCO | Perception/autonomy bolt-on; less need for a berry fleet | 2029-2031 | Low | S101 |
| Berry marketer | Driscoll's, California Giant, Naturipe (private) | Harvest security and grower data; no public robotics M&A record | 2029-2031 | Low | S95 (unverified) |
| Indoor grower | Oishii (private) | IP and team; bought Tortuga 2025-03; indoor focus | 2028-2030 | Low-medium | S93, S144 |

### The precedent record separates platform exits from harvesting assets

Blue River was bought for $305M at 3.5x its $87M post-money, with $30M+ raised and See & Spray launched; Bear Flag for $250M after a $7.9M seed, 31.6x the seed, before commercial scale. CNH paid $2.1B EV for Raven at a 33.6% premium; AGCO paid $2.0B for 85% of Trimble Ag at an implied $2.35B EV and 13.8x 2023E EBITDA; Kubota paid $73M for AgJunction. Harvesting outcomes are smaller: Root AI went to AppHarvest for $60M in 2021; Advanced Farm raised $25M, ceased operations in July 2025 and sold its IP and team to CNH for undisclosed terms; Tortuga deployed $50M and 150 robots and sold its IP and team to Oishii in 2025-03, also undisclosed. No harvesting-robot company in the set has sold for $100M+. [S98, S96, S118, S99, S101, S104, S32, S28, S97, S93, S144]

### The base rate is two $100M+ exits in eight, and none in harvesting

Of the eight venture-backed ag-robotics companies in the comparison set, two reached a $100M+ exit (Blue River, Bear Flag) — 25% — but both were autonomy platforms; of the five harvesting-robot companies (Harvest CROO, Advanced Farm, Tortuga, Tevel, Orrin), none did, and the only disclosed harvesting exit is Root AI at $60M. At the $90M post-money the lead owns 13.33%: a $100M exit returns 1.1x before the Series B and 1.0x after 20% dilution, when the preference binds; $250M returns 2.8x and 2.2x. The distribution is 18% at $250M, 40% at $100M and 42% at $25M: 0.18 × 2.2 + 0.40 × 1.0 + 0.42 × 0.59 = 1.04x. The $25M bear is an equity exit on the deck's pari passu terms, not a blended asset-sale recovery: the lead takes 32.6% of the $36.77M stack, about $7.1M, after fleet debt and costs. A $12-40M asset sale returns less; senior or 2x notes would cut the $25M recovery to 0.21x and a $10M senior 2028 round to 0.31x — structure cases, not the base distribution. Below $90M the preference, not the operating plan, sets the return: the first $36.77M of equity goes to the stack, which means a technically good 2027 season still returns only capital. The counter-case is a $250-305M Deere or CNH bid for the team and perception model, as at Blue River and Bear Flag; at 95% pick rates and 360 robots a $250M+ bid is possible, and the 2-of-8 rate is a small, survivor-biased set. [S98, S96, S32, S29, S28, S93, S108, S95]

### The Series B test is the 2028 plan plus a 7x multiple

A 2028 Series B above the $72M pre-money requires the company to beat, not just meet, the plan. The 2027 plan is 360 robots, $5.6M revenue, 52% RaaS gross margin and $8M ARR on the company's definition; the 2028 plan is $13.2M revenue and 61% gross margin (company-provided and unverified). At 5-7x forward revenue the 2028 plan is worth $66-92M pre-money, so a flat round needs the full plan and a 7x multiple; above $90M needs $18M+ of 2028 revenue at 5x. On 2027 revenue alone, even 10x gives $56M — below the current mark. The test is $13.2M+ of 2028 revenue, 60%+ gross margin, 360+ robots in service, 80%+ renewal of the 2026 paying growers and unit cost below $36,000. If the company hits only the 2027 plan, the 2028 Series B is likely a down round. [S95]
